newsitem.title: USA: Brooklyn girl wins spelling bee in a shout.
newsitem.headline: Brooklyn girl wins spelling bee in a shout.

text.p: Rebecca Sealfon, a nervous but exuberant 13-year-old from Brooklyn, won the National Spelling Bee Thursday by shouting out the correct spelling of "euonym," a word meaning a well-suited description.

She outlasted 244 other finalists, in the end going head-to-head for eight rounds with Prem Trivedi, a slight, 11-year-old boy from Howell, N.J. He finally stumbled on "cortile," a word meaning a courtyard surrounded by building walls to which he added an extra "l."
"It's an incredible amount of luck," as well as constant study, said Sealfon after it was over, admitting that at least one of her earlier answers was a lucky guess.

Through the contest she nervously threw her arms around herself, repeatedly asking for definitions and roots of words, and asking herself if she was hearing the words correctly. She even sat out several earlier rounds on the sidelines, appearing to be too stressed to be on the stage.

But she finished with a bang, not even asking for definitions for the last two words -- "coterie" and finally "euonym," whose letters she shouted out one by one, flapping her arms and jumping up and down.

The 70th annual contest was sponsored by Scripps Howard newspapers and brought contestants ranging in age from 9 to 15 from from around the country sponsored by newspapers in their localities. Seventeen of the contestants -- including Sealfon -- attended school at home.
She was sponsored by the New York Daily News.

The final rounds of the two-day contest began the afternoon with more than a dozen survivors, but they were quickly weeded out by a minefield of words like "passementerie" (a braided edging), "souterrain" (an underground chamber) and "entrecote" (a steak cut from between the ribs).
Sealfon herself tripped once in the final rounds against Trivedi on "dulcinea," meaning a mistress or sweetheart, but under the rules each of the final contestants was allowed one fall.

After Trivedi, who was sponsored by the Asbury Park Press, missed a second word Sealfon correctly spelled the next and winning one. Her reward was $5,000 cash prize, a loving cup, a $1,000 bond, a laptop computer -- and an electronic dictionary-thesaurus.
Sealfon, whose father is a neurologist-neurobiologist, was a veteran of the spelling wars, having placed eighth in last year's contest.
